section_summary: This section closes a statistical bulletin on United States exports of strategic war materials to Japan, then documents mounting public and official pressure for embargoes through petitions, advocacy reports, congressional correspondence, Chinese appeals, and press commentary. A substantial group of memoranda examines Japan’s dependence on American petroleum, aviation gasoline, metals, and refining technology, including the State Department’s application of its “moral embargo.” The section also records commercial inquiries about antimony, tin, iso-octane, cracking plants, and technical assistance to Japanese industry.

keywords: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression

subfiles.title: Sales of War Materials by the United States to Japan, First Eight Months of 1939—conclusion and appendices
subfiles.from: Hu Tun-yuan, Chinese Council for Economic Research
subfiles.about: The bulletin analyzes American exports of strategic materials to Japan and supplies comparative trade tables for 1937–1939.
subfiles.summary: The concluding analysis emphasizes Japan’s dependence on American scrap iron, machine tools, copper, ferro-alloys, petroleum, aircraft parts, and other strategic commodities. It argues that American machinery enabled Japanese import substitution while the 1938 aviation “moral embargo” sharply reduced finished-aircraft exports. Appendices quantify the United States’ share of Japan’s war-related imports and Japanese gold and silver shipments to the United States.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Chinese Council for Economic Research Bulletin No. 16
subfiles.to: Chinese Ambassador to the United States
subfiles.about: Hornbeck thanks the ambassador for three copies of the bulletin on American sales of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges receipt of Bulletin No. 16, covering January–August 1939 and comparing the same periods of 1938 and 1937. He expresses appreciation for the ambassador’s courtesy in making the copies available.

subfiles.title: Telegram requesting action on the Philippine embargo petition
subfiles.from: Philippine Committee for Embargo Against Japan
subfiles.about: The committee asks the president to act on a 48,000-signature petition for an embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram states that Commissioner Sayre forwarded the petition to the State Department. It argues that embargo action would protect American democracy and interests in the Orient.

subfiles.title: Forwarding the Philippine Committee’s telegram
subfiles.from: Henry F. Grady, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards the Philippine Committee’s telegram for whatever action the Interior Department considers appropriate.
subfiles.summary: Grady recalls the Department’s December 1, 1939 correspondence about a Philippine petition bearing more than 48,000 signatures. He encloses the telegram sent to the president concerning the requested embargo on war materials for Japan.

subfiles.title: Transmittal concerning the League for the Defense of Democracy
subfiles.to: United States High Commissioner to the Philippine Islands
subfiles.about: The Department sends League for the Defense of Democracy materials and explains the handling of its cable and petition.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses a January 29 letter and report sent to the president by the Manila organization. It also supplies the Department’s December 1 reply concerning the earlier petition filed with the High Commissioner.
keywords: League for the Defense of Democracy

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing the American Committee’s progress report
subfiles.about: Price sends Hamilton a report on the progress and program of the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression.
subfiles.summary: Price explains that the report was prepared for contributors to the committee’s work. He encloses a copy in the belief that the State Department will find it useful.

subfiles.title: Progress and Program of the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The report describes the committee’s organization, publicity work, finances, Washington relations, and proposed campaign through June 1940.
subfiles.summary: The committee recounts its growth from August 1938 into a national campaign seeking to halt American credits and war supplies to Japan. It details leadership, local committees, publications, mailings, speaking engagements, press and radio work, and evidence of increasingly pro-embargo public opinion. Audited statements and internal accounts cover income and expenditure from 1938 through February 1940, while the final pages propose a twenty-week program requiring approximately $55,418 in special contributions.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the American Committee’s report
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Price’s letter and the enclosed report on the committee’s progress and program.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton thanks Price for making a copy of the report available to the State Department. The brief reply formally records its receipt.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on further letters from Chengtu
subfiles.to: Department of State file and officers
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends ending substantive correspondence with Marshal Chou and S. C. Liao after a third appeal from Chengtu.
subfiles.summary: The writer notes that the Embassy had been instructed to answer two previous letters. The memorandum suggests that the June 1 letter and any later communications from the two Chinese leaders be filed without further acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Appeal from the Chengtu Association of Gentry after Japanese bombing
subfiles.from: C. K. Chou and S. C. Liao, Chengtu Association of Gentry
subfiles.about: Chou and Liao appeal for an end to American oil and iron sales that sustain Japan’s bombing campaign in China.
subfiles.summary: The letter describes heavy civilian, student, and teacher casualties in Japanese attacks on Chongqing educational institutions. It argues that Japan’s costly war could not continue without foreign supplies and identifies the United States as its principal remaining source. The authors ask Hull to persuade American merchants to stop the trade, invoking the gratitude of Sichuan’s population.

subfiles.title: Earlier Chengtu Association appeal against aid to Japan
subfiles.from: C. K. Chou and S. C. Liao, Chengtu Association of Gentry
subfiles.about: The association urges the United States to express sympathy for China by halting material assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Although badly degraded by OCR, the letter presents Japanese aggression as a danger to international peace and contrasts American sympathy for China with continuing supplies to Japan. Chou and Liao ask that such assistance be brought to a complete halt.

subfiles.title: Instruction to acknowledge the January 10 Chengtu letter
subfiles.about: The Department asks the ambassador to acknowledge the Chengtu Association of Gentry’s January 10 letter.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses the letter from C. K. Chou and S. C. Liao. The ambassador may state that its contents have been noted and that the spirit prompting it is appreciated.

subfiles.title: Summary of Commerce Department findings on Japan’s petroleum position
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes Secretary Hopkins’s material on Japan’s dependence on American petroleum and aviation gasoline.
subfiles.summary: It states that Japan depended almost entirely on the United States for high-octane aviation gasoline, while imports had probably filled most available storage. Japan possessed refining capacity, alternative crude sources, and tankers, but substitution would raise costs and reduce efficiency. An American cutoff would handicap Japan in a major-power war, though existing stocks could sustain the China conflict for at least another year.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department transmittal of petroleum memorandum
subfiles.from: Harry L. Hopkins, Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.about: Hopkins transmits a memorandum concerning Japan’s petroleum industry and dependence on American supplies.
subfiles.summary: Much of the letter is illegible, but its enclosure and later acknowledgment identify the subject as Japanese petroleum. The accompanying analysis was forwarded for State Department consideration.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Secretary Hopkins on Japan’s dependence on aviation gasoline—first copy
subfiles.about: Young assesses Japan’s access to high-octane aviation gasoline, crude petroleum, refining capacity, and reserve stocks.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum concludes that Japan was effectively dependent on the United States for 87- to 100-octane gasoline, although it could obtain lower-grade fuels and crude elsewhere. Alternative supplies and Japan’s tanker fleet would allow continued operations, but at higher cost and reduced refining efficiency. A table estimates Japanese crude-oil and gasoline availability and the American share for 1937–1940.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Secretary Hopkins on Japan’s dependence on aviation gasoline—duplicate copy
subfiles.about: This duplicate copy analyzes Japan’s petroleum imports, high-octane fuel dependence, refinery capacity, and ability to withstand an American cutoff.
subfiles.summary: Young finds that the United States was virtually Japan’s sole source of high-octane aviation gasoline and supplied most imported crude oil. Japan could obtain lower-grade petroleum from the Netherlands Indies, British Borneo, Sakhalin, Latin America, and Bahrain, but its refineries were optimized for California crude. He estimates that existing stocks would permit another year of war in China without a serious petroleum shortage.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the Commerce Department petroleum memorandum
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Hopkins’s letter and the enclosed memorandum on the Japanese petroleum industry.
subfiles.summary: Hull describes the memorandum as very interesting. He expresses appreciation for its receipt.

subfiles.title: White House referral slip to the State Department
subfiles.to: Officials of the Department of State
subfiles.about: The slip refers attached correspondence to State Department officials.
subfiles.summary: The page is a brief administrative referral rather than substantive correspondence. It appears to route the following congressional letter concerning arms shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Congressman Hare’s transmittal of an anti-arms-shipment letter
subfiles.about: Hare forwards Carrie McCully Patrick’s protest against shipping arms and munitions from the United States to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hare states that he is strongly sympathetic to Patrick’s suggestions. He submits her enclosed letter to the president for consideration.

subfiles.title: Correction of January 1940 high-test gasoline export figures
subfiles.about: Hornbeck corrects his earlier warning about an apparent surge in January aviation-gasoline exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Commerce Department figures had initially suggested that January 1940 exports nearly equaled all of 1939. Hornbeck reports that the figures were wholly erroneous and that the corrected quantity was about one twenty-fourth of the 1939 total. He adds a skeptical comment about citing Commerce statistics in the future.

subfiles.title: Corrected January aviation-gasoline export statistics
subfiles.from: H. W. Moseley, Division of Controls
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck; copy to Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Moseley reports corrected Commerce Department figures for January 1940 gasoline exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Paul L. Hopper explains that the preliminary figure of 460,000 barrels was actually the dollar valuation. The corrected aviation-gasoline quantity was 23,976 barrels, compared with 562,230 barrels during 1939. Regular-gasoline exports in January were reported as 95,202 barrels.

subfiles.title: Chinese newspaper editorials urging an American embargo
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Embassy at Chungking
subfiles.about: Johnson summarizes two Chinese editorials advocating a United States embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The China Times argues that Japan’s search for alternative raw materials and diplomatic maneuvering should not deter prompt American action. The Japan Central Daily News lists seven reasons for congressional delay but dismisses fears of war, a Japanese-Soviet alliance, or lost trade. Both editorials maintain that only a decisive embargo would restrain Japan.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about exporting bonded Chinese antimony to Japan
subfiles.about: Allen records a company inquiry concerning the proposed export of twenty-five tons of Chinese antimony to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Biscaye of C. Tennant Sons & Co. argued that bonded antimony could be sold to Mitsui without paying import duty and described prior shipments as normal trade. Allen explained that such an export would conflict with the Army and Navy Munitions Board’s strategic-materials policy and could not reasonably be called normal peacetime commerce. Biscaye appeared willing to abandon the transaction and submit details of earlier exports.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Morito Morishima on the Japan Gasoline Company contract
subfiles.about: Hamilton records Morishima’s request for favorable treatment of part of the Japan Gasoline Company’s contract with Universal Oil Products.
subfiles.summary: Morishima asked whether the Department had decided to permit partial fulfillment of the contract. Hamilton replied that the government could not give a favorable response and that its position remained that stated in the reply to the Japanese Embassy’s January 6 note on moral embargoes.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo enclosing the Morishima conversation
subfiles.about: The Department sends Tokyo a copy of the March 5 conversation concerning the Universal Oil Products contract.
subfiles.summary: The instruction refers to the February 29 instruction and earlier correspondence on the Japan Gasoline Company contract. It encloses the memorandum of Hamilton’s conversation with the Japanese Embassy counselor for the ambassador’s information.

subfiles.title: Report of commercial iso-octane delivered for export to Japan
subfiles.about: Adams reports the February delivery of 2,500 drums of commercial iso-octane to Mitsui for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The shipment consisted of 2,500 drums, each holding fifty-three gallons. The letter was submitted as a factual report to the Division of Controls.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the February iso-octane report
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges Adams’s report of iso-octane sold and delivered for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply records receipt of the March 5 letter concerning the February 1940 transaction. Yost expresses the Department’s appreciation for the information.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about exporting tin to Japan
subfiles.about: Allen records an Associated Metals and Minerals Corporation inquiry about restrictions on tin exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Allen explained the government’s policy toward strategic materials and said that exporting tin to Japan would be inconsistent with it. The company representative indicated that the tin would not be sold for Japanese export.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to “The New Outlook in the Far East in the Light of the European War”
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression, Roger S. Greene
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a document quoting a pamphlet about American influence and threats to stop supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The referenced paper requested verification of statements about the importance of American leverage over Japan. The original was filed under number 711.94/1443.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to a proposed United Engineering installation in Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report that a successful Stupino installation might lead to a similar United Engineering and Foundry plant in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Cummings said negotiations for the Japanese installation had reached an advanced stage. He could not confirm whether a contract had been signed, and the original report was filed under 861.24/420.

subfiles.title: South Carolina concurrent resolution on America’s economic role in the war in China
subfiles.to: Congress of the United States; Cordell Hull; South Carolina congressional delegation
subfiles.about: The resolution asks Congress to examine whether American trade is materially aiding Japanese aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: Following an address by medical missionary Walter Judd, the assembly concluded that the United States was supplying Japan with materials necessary for war. It questioned whether American conduct was truly neutral or instead gave aid and comfort to China’s aggressor. Copies were ordered sent to Hull and South Carolina’s senators and representatives.

subfiles.title: Congressman Kunkel’s appeal to end war-material sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Kunkel asks Hull to end the policy of selling war materials to Japan and explain why it has continued.
subfiles.summary: Kunkel says he had previously defended State Department discretion against demands for a legislated embargo. Constituents’ protests and his own judgment now lead him to condemn American material aid to the aggressor in China. He requests an explanation of the policy’s basis and likely duration.

subfiles.title: Hull’s reply to Congressman Kunkel
subfiles.about: Hull explains the lack of statutory authority for a broad embargo and points to existing moral-embargo measures.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that the Neutrality Act of 1939 did not authorize prohibiting arms exports and that, apart from tin-plate scrap and helium, no law permitted bans on other important war materials. New legislation would therefore be necessary for a formal embargo. He encloses the president’s December 2 statement and December press releases concerning aircraft, aeronautical materials, and high-quality aviation-gasoline technology.

subfiles.title: Treadway’s transmittal of H. F. Misener’s protest
subfiles.about: Treadway forwards a constituent’s protest against shipping war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The congressman encloses H. F. Misener’s March 16 letter for State Department information and consideration. The cover letter contains no separate policy recommendation.

subfiles.title: H. F. Misener’s protest against supplying Japan
subfiles.about: Misener asks Treadway to stop American shipments of scrap iron, gasoline, aircraft, and similar supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Misener expresses deep concern about continued American commerce with Japan. He characterizes the war against the Chinese people as brutality and asks the congressman to use every available means to stop it.

subfiles.title: Hull’s reply to Treadway concerning Misener’s embargo request
subfiles.about: Hull replies that no statute authorizes the embargo advocated by Misener and encloses statements on existing moral-embargo policy.
subfiles.summary: Hull says new legislation would be required before the proposed embargo could take effect. He supplies the president’s December 2, 1939 statement and December press releases concerning aircraft exports and the transfer of high-quality aviation-gasoline production technology. Misener’s original letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Technical explanation of gasoline production and high-grade aviation fuel
subfiles.from: H. J. Halle, Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.about: Halle explains gasoline-production processes and asks the Department to evaluate whether its moral-embargo policy should extend beyond iso-octane plants.
subfiles.summary: The letter distinguishes straight-run, cracked, reformed, catalytically cracked, polymer, iso-octane, and other aviation-gasoline components. It compares national understandings of “high grade” aviation gasoline and explains blending, hydrogenation, and tetraethyl-lead use. Halle notes that Universal Oil Products was constructing plants in the Soviet Union and Japan and had interpreted departmental correspondence as allowing additional cracking units.

subfiles.title: Green’s clarification of the Department’s position on cracking units
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Green clarifies that the State Department neither approved nor disapproved Universal Oil Products’ proposed additional cracking units in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges Halle’s technical account of gasoline production. He reiterates that companies possessing the technical information must judge whether a transaction contravenes the government’s policy against transferring high-quality aviation-gasoline technology. The Department permits or refuses commercial transactions only as provided by law.

subfiles.title: Halle’s acknowledgment of Green’s clarification
subfiles.about: Halle confirms that Universal Oil Products’ understanding accords with the Department’s interpretation.
subfiles.summary: Halle thanks Green for the February 8 letter. He states that the company did not intend to misinterpret the earlier departmental correspondence.

subfiles.title: Telephone inquiry about extending the aviation-gasoline moral embargo
subfiles.about: Green records L. N. Healy’s inquiry about a proposed meeting of oil companies to broaden the moral embargo on aviation-gasoline technology.
subfiles.summary: Healy asked whether the Department had acted on Halle’s suggestion for another meeting with interested petroleum firms. Green replied that the proposal remained under consideration and that Halle would be informed if the Department decided to proceed.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Universal Oil Products representatives on aviation-gasoline technology
subfiles.about: The memorandum begins an account of a meeting with Universal Oil Products officers concerning Halle’s technical letter and the aviation-gasoline moral embargo.
subfiles.summary: H. J. Halle, Gustav Egloff, and L. N. Healy met with State Department officials Joseph C. Green and Mr. Henderson. Halle asked whether the technical information in his January 30 letter had interested the Department, and Green answered affirmatively. The discussion of moral-embargo restrictions continues beyond this section.
